hints: Compare the sizes of the structures in the top diagram. Which ones are large and dense, like the nucleus and nucleolus, and which ones are tiny and thin, like RER, Golgi and small vesicles?
Remember what a simple unstained light microscope can do. Its resolution limit is about $200 \text{ nm}$ and with daylight only there is no stain to add contrast, so which organelles will disappear?
walkthrough:
**Look at what the electron microscope shows**

Lovely start. The top diagram shows lots of detail. You can see the nucleus with its dark nucleolus, plus rough ER, Golgi body, a mitochondrion, ribosomes and small vesicles.

That is because an electron microscope has very high resolution, about $0.1 \text{ nm}$.

**Apply the light microscope limit**

Now think like the light microscope. A light microscope has a much lower resolution, about $200 \text{ nm}$, so tiny membranes are not resolved.

Even more important, this is a simple microscope with daylight only and no stain. Unstained cytoplasm and membranes have almost no contrast, so small organelles become invisible.

**Decide what is left visible**

The only large, dense structures with enough natural contrast are the nucleus and the darker nucleolus inside it.

So the same cell will look almost empty except for the grey nucleus with its black dot. That matches A perfectly.

options.A: Correct and reassuring. It shows only the cell surface, cytoplasm, nucleus and nucleolus, which are the only structures large and contrasted enough to see unstained with light.
options.B: Not quite. It still shows Golgi body, vesicles and RER fragments, which are far too small and low contrast to see without electron microscopy and staining.
options.C: Good try, but it still shows a mitochondrion with cristae, Golgi and vesicles. Those details need the high resolution of the electron microscope.
options.D: Close look shows RER with ribosomes and a mitochondrion around the nucleus. Those membranes are invisible in an unstained light microscope, so this is too detailed.
